A.Y. Salehuzzaman, Assit. Attorney-General  ----- For the Appellant.

full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff's case in brief, was that while he was serving under the then Government of East Pakistan as an Assistant Director of Health Services, East Pakistan, Malariology, Dacca he was served with notice dated 19-3-1959 by the Chairman, Screening Committee headed by Mr DK Power, asking him to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken against him for unsatisfactory service and for misconduct and he was also asked to appear before the committee at 8 AM on 28-3-1959 in the room of the Chairman. Thereupon the plaintiff submitted an explanation wherein he denied the charge made against him. He prayed to the screening Committee for having a written, specific and definite charge but he was not supplied with any specific and definite charge. The Screening Committee in utter violation of the mandatory provisions of Public Conduct (Scrutiny) Ordinance, 1956 and the Rules framed there under give its findings and recommendations without giving the plaintiff any opportunity to defend himself and recommended for his compulsory retirement. The plaintiff held an appeal before the Secretary Health and LSG Department, Govt of East Pakistan which was sent to the Advisory Committee for consideration but the Advisory Committee also found against the plaintiff. Ultimately by an order dated 3-6-59 the plaintiff was compulsorily retired from service for misconduct. The plain-tiff thereafter brought this suit for declaration as aforesaid. 

 3. The defendant Government contested the suit by denying the allegations of the plain-tiff and contending, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable and the impugned order of compulsory retirement could not be questioned before the Court. 

 4. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge after a careful consideration of the evidence on record, the circumstances of the case and the legal question involved decreed the suit declaring that the findings and recommendations of the Screening Committee dated 144-1959 and the order compulsory retirement dated 3-6-59 were illegal, ultra vires, void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff. It was further declared that the plaintiff was still in service in the cadre of an Assistant Director of Health Services under the Public Health and ISG Department, Government of East Pakistan. Being aggrieved, the defendant Government has preferred this appeal. 

 The learned Assistant Attorney-General has mainly relied on the case reported in 21 DLR (SC) 16 (Government of East Pakistan vs Mr Murzuqullah and four others) and 25 DLR (SC) 94 (Bangladesh subscribed in place of province of East Pakistan vs Naziruddin Ahmed) and has contended that since the plaintiff Government servant was compulsorily retired under sub-clause (b) clause (5) of Article 6 of the Laws (Continuance in Force) Order, 1958 which was a super-constitutional law, the legality of the impugned order could not be questioned before any Court. He has contended that under sub-clause (b) of clause (5) of Article 6 of the said Order, no enquiry was at all necessary and the opportunity of enquiry that was given to the plaintiff was merely gratuitous. Mr MH Khandker, the learned Counsel has distinguished the facts of the present case from the facts of these two reported cases relied on by the learned Assistant Attorney-General and has relied n the cases reported in DLR (SC) 9 (Zafar-ul-Ahsan vs The Republic Pakistan) and PLD 1963 (SC) 185 (The Province of East Pakistan and another vs M Amir Hossain). The cases relied on by the learned Assistant Attorney-General were cases in which the officer concerned was compulsorily retired on the ground of inefficiency. Mr Khandker has contended that the present case was distinguishable from those cases inasmuch, in the present case the plaintiff Government servant was compulsorily retired on a charge of misconduct Relying on Zafar-ul-Ahsan's and Amir Hossain's cases, the learned Counsel has contended that the impugned order could not be sustained in law and that the bar of jurisdiction of Courts did not apply. 

 6. Clauses (3), (4) and (5) of Article 6 of the Laws (Continuance in Force) Order, 1958 (hereinafter referred to as the Order), as they stood at the material time, are as follows:— 

 (a) suspended, reduced in rank, removed or dismissed for being corrupt or for misconduct, or for inefficiency after such enquiry as may be held under the orders of the Central Government, or 

 7. On a reading of the provision of sub-clause (b) of clause (5), it is clear that for the purpose of retiring any person for any cause mentioned in sub-clause (a) which includes "misconduct" no enquiry was necessary provided the order made before 1-7-59. The impugned order is dated 3-6-59, that is, before 1-7-59. If the principle enunciated in Marzupullas' and Naziruddin's Case would apply to the present case, it can at once be concluded that the enquiry held in the case was merely gratuitous and that the impugned order could not be questioned before any Court. Mr MH Khandaker has, however, pointed out that in the above two cases, enquiry was held into a charge of inefficiency, "inefficiency" having ceased to be a ground for enquiry under the Public Conduct (Scrutiny) Ordinance, 1959 since 28-2-59 and the Court held that the enquiry was not a statutory enquiry but merely an enquiry held at the request of the Governor and was gratuitous. But in the case before us the enquiry was into a charge of "misconduct" and the Screening Committee had jurisdiction to hold enquiry into a charge of misconduct under the Public Conduct (Scrutiny) Ordinance, 1959. It was, therefore, a statutory enquiry. Being statutory enquiry, the Screening Committee was bound to hold enquiry in accordance with law and if it has not done so, its findings and recommendations are bad in law and any order of the Authority based on such findings and recommendations is also bad in law and cannot be sustained. In support of his contention he has placed the two decisions already referred. In Zafar-ul Ahsan's case the Supreme Court of Pakistan has held that though for the action taken no enquiry was necessary but the Government having ordered a statutory enquiry relatable under the Public Conduct (Scrutiny) Ordinance, 1959 and the Rules made thereunder the enquiry was bound to follow the statutory procedure and an omission to comply with such procedure in some material respect would have vitiated the result of the enquiry. Mr Zafar-ul-Ahsan's case, however, failed on the ground that the Court had no jurisdiction to question the order. However, this ruling is an authority for the proposition that even when an enquiry is not necessary under the law but if the Government has ordered an enquiry under the provision of a statute the procedure laid down therein has to be followed and if the procedure is not followed the enquiry is vitiated and any punishment based on the result of the enquiry will be vitiated. In Amir Hossain's case, the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that the order retiring the public servant for misconduct cannot be questioned in any court, but to attract this bar misconduct must be found and if it is found that the matters on which the public servant was found to be guilty of misconduct are insufficient (to sustain such findings then the finding of the Screening Committee and the order of the Authority on the basis of that findings cannot be sustained. 

 9. It is patent that the alleged adverse remarks for the years 1950-55 and 1957 including those specifically mentioned by the Screening committee are of very general nature and vague. There is no allegation of any specific act substantiated by any specific instances. It was the positive averment of the plaintiff that these adverse remarks were never communicated to him and he had no opportunity to represent against them and this has not been denied. Even at the stage of enquiry the plaintiff asked for specific charge (Exhibit 3), but the screening committee never supplied him with any. The plaintiff had also challenged these adverse remarks as malafide and rom. He has alleged that the adverse remarks have been given by Dr Md Fahimuddin and Dr MA Jabbar who bore grudge against the plaintiff and some of them were prepared in one sitting. We do not want to go into this question of malafide and rom. We are however, of opinion that the remarks of the Annual Confidential Reports on which the finding of misconduct has been arrived at by the screening committee are too vague and insufficient on which a finding of misconduct could be based. "Adverse remark" in the ACRS are opinions of the Reporting Officers and can hardly be treated as evidence of any misconduct which may be constituted only by specific and definite acts, done contrary to rules regulating the conduct of Government servants or which are unbecoming of an officer. we have already noticed that the adverse were not substantiated by any specific instance and they were vague. We are of the view that the finding of the Screening Committee that the plaintiff was guilty of misconduct is not based on any material. In this view of matter we are of the opinion that the principle enunciated in Amir Hossain's case applies in the present case with all force. The matter before us admits of argument that the materials on which the respondent was found by the Screening Committee to be guilty of misconduct are wholly insufficient to sustain the charge of misconduct. As to the question whether the jurisdiction of the court is barred under Article 6(5) (b) of the Order, we hold, relying on Amir Hossain's case, that to attract this bar, "misconduct" must be found at the very least in logic and here as in the reported decision nonsequiter is plain. Under section 10 of the Public Conduct (Scrutiny) Ordinance, 1959 the order or finding by an appointing authority or Screening Committee cannot for the same reasons as before the finding in this case is no finding which protection against Judicial examination can be claimed and the order which proceeded therein is equally liable to interference. In Zafar-ul Ahsan's case it was laid down that it a statute provides that an order made by an authority acting under it shall not be called in question in any court, all that is necessary to oust the jurisdictions of the Courts is that the authority should have been constituted as required by the statute the person proceeded against should be subject to the jurisdiction of the authority, the ground on which action is taken should be within the grounds stated by the statute and the order made should be such as could have been made under the statute. In the present case, the first, second and fourth conditions are fulfilled, but the third condition, namely that the ground on which action is taken should be within the grounds stated by the statute is not fulfilled. It is true that the action has been taken on the purported ground of misconduct and misconduct is a ground stated in the statute, but we have already seen that in the present case "misconduct" could not be found and non-sequiter is plain. We are, there-fore, of the opinion that the impugned order passed under Article 6(5) (b) of the Order, was liable to be questioned before a court and bar to jurisdiction does not apply. It may be stated that in Amir Hossain's case, the principle enunciated in Zafar-ul Ahsan's case was duly considered. The present case is on all fours, with Amir Hossain's case and we feel no hesitation to apply that principle in the present case. 

 10. The learned Assistant Attorney-General has argued that the Laws (Continuance in Force) Order 1958 was a super-constitutional law and action taken thereunder could not be questioned before Court, the question before us is not whether the laws (Continuances in Force) order is a super constitutional or supra-constitutional law qua the late constitution of 1956 (At the relevant period the country was being governed as nearly as may be in accordance with the late, Constitution by virtue of Article 2 of the laws (Continuance in Force) Order or whether the said Order was the transitional constitution of the relevant period but the question before us is whether the impugned action was within the scope and authority of the said very Order and whether it could be questioned before a Court. We have already found that the impugned action was beyond the scope of the order as because the ground of "Misconduct" on which action was taken on the authority of the order did not exist even in logic, and that bar of jurisdiction of courts did not apply. In this view of the matter, the contention of the learned Assistant Attorney-General must fall. 

 11. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge came to a finding that the findings and recommendations of the Screening Committee were ultra vires and without jurisdiction and the impugned order of compulsory retirement of the plaintiff and respondent on the basis of the findings are recommendations of the Screening Committee was also illegal and ultra vires, void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff. We find no reason to differ with him. We have already found that the provision relating to bar to jurisdiction of Court does not apply in the facts and circumstances of the present case. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge has further declared that the plaintiff is still in service in the cadre of an Assistant Director of Health Services under the Public Health and LSG Department, Government of East Pakistan. With the emergence of Bangladesh Government of East Pakistan and the Department of Public Health and LSG of that Government are no longer in existence. This part of the declaration can only be to the effect that the plaintiff shall be deemed to be in service in the cadre of an Assistant Director of Health Services under the Public Health Department of the Government of the then East Pakistan as on the date of institution of the suit.
